Brand colors represent the core visual identity of Biamp within the SOLAR Design System.
They are used to reinforce brand recognition across products, marketing surfaces, and key interface elements.

Brand tokens provide a consistent way to apply Biamp’s primary brand palette while ensuring predictable behavior across light and dark themes.

Brand colors should be used intentionally and sparingly, typically for primary brand moments, highlights, or branded surfaces rather than general UI structure.
Primary brand color used for key brand moments, highlights, and brand-aligned UI elements.
Secondary brand color used for supporting brand accents and contrast with the primary brand color.
Neutral brand color used for branded surfaces or backgrounds where a lighter brand presence is needed.

Core surface tokens define the foundational background layers of the interface. They establish spatial hierarchy, elevation logic, and layout structure across light and dark modes.

Core surface tokens are role-based and independent of components. They define how content is layered — from base application background to raised or interactive surfaces — ensuring consistent contrast and structural rhythm.
Primary content containers and default component surfaces.
Elevated surfaces such as cards, panels, or overlays.
The highest surface level for floating and temporary interface elements.
Surface used for high-contrast or inverted contexts.
Interactive surface highlight on pointer hover.
Persistent active/selected state on interactive surfaces.
Background surface for dialogs, drawers, and modal overlays.
Subdued surface for de-emphasized content areas.
Semi-transparent overlay behind modals and drawers.

Feedback surfaces provide contextual background colors used to communicate system states and user feedback. Subtle variants use light tints for inline alerts, banners, and notifications. Strong variants use saturated fills for high-emphasis badges, tags, and status indicators. Both ensure accessible contrast and visual consistency.
Subtle background for success messages, alerts, and confirmations.
Subtle background for warnings and caution states.
Subtle background for errors and critical issues.
Subtle background for neutral and default feedback states.
Strong saturated background for high-emphasis success indicators.
Strong saturated background for high-emphasis warning indicators.
Strong saturated background for high-emphasis danger indicators.
Strong saturated background for high-emphasis info indicators.
Strong saturated background for high-emphasis neutral indicators.
Medium-emphasis surface for success notices and confirmations.
Medium-emphasis surface for warnings and cautionary states.
Medium-emphasis surface for errors and critical issues.
Medium-emphasis surface for neutral and default feedback states.

So, regarding the border colors. You border tokens define structural boundaries and visual separation across the interface. They establish levels of emphasis — from subtle containment to strong delineation and interactive focus — ensuring clarity and consistent definition across all surfaces.

Border tokens are role-based and independent of components, allowing structural hierarchy to scale reliably across themes and layouts.
Border for inactive or unavailable elements.
Border color used on dark or contrasting surfaces.
Hover-state border color, between subtle and strong.
Flush border that blends with the page surface.

Feedback border tokens express semantic states through structural emphasis. They signal validation and status — success, warning, danger, or informational — across interactive components. These tokens work in coordination with feedback text and surface tokens to ensure consistent hierarchy, contrast, and accessibility.
Low-emphasis focus border for interactive elements.
High-emphasis focus border for inputs and critical elements.
Low-emphasis success border for containers and backgrounds.
High-emphasis success border for inputs and critical elements.
Low-emphasis warning border for containers and backgrounds.
High-emphasis warning border for inputs and critical elements.
Low-emphasis info border for containers and backgrounds.
High-emphasis info border for inputs and critical elements.
Low-emphasis danger border for containers and backgrounds.
High-emphasis danger border for inputs and critical elements.
Medium-emphasis border for error and critical states.
Subtle border for neutral and default feedback states.
Medium-emphasis border for neutral and default feedback states.
Strong border for neutral and default feedback states.

Core text tokens define the visual hierarchy of written content across the interface. They establish levels of emphasis — from primary content to supporting and disabled states — ensuring clarity, readability, and consistent contrast across all surface levels. Core text tokens are role-based and independent of components, allowing content to scale reliably across themes and layouts.
The default text color for main content and essential information.
A lower-emphasis text color used for supporting or contextual information.
A subtle text color for metadata, hints, or non-critical details.
A text color used for inactive or unavailable content.
Text color used on dark or high-contrast surfaces.

Feedback text tokens communicate status and system meaning within contextual components such as alerts, inline messages, and notifications. Unlike core text tokens, which express hierarchy, feedback text tokens convey semantic intent — success, error, warning, or informational states. They are always paired with corresponding feedback surfaces to maintain clarity, accessibility, and visual consistency.
Text used to communicate positive status, confirmation, or successful outcomes within inline feedback and system messages.
Text used to signal caution, potential risk, or situations requiring user attention.
Text used to communicate errors, critical issues, or destructive outcomes.
Text used to present neutral or informational messages that provide context or guidance.
Text color for neutral feedback messages.

Core icon tokens define the visual hierarchy of iconography across the interface. They establish levels of emphasis — from primary interactive icons to supporting and disabled states — ensuring clarity, consistency, and accessible contrast across all surface levels.  Core icon tokens are role-based and independent of components, allowing icons to scale reliably across themes, layouts, and densities.
The default icon color for key actions and primary visual emphasis.
A lower-emphasis icon color used for supporting or contextual actions.
A subtle icon color for decorative or low-priority indicators.
An icon color used for inactive or unavailable controls.
Icon color used on dark or high-contrast surfaces.

Feedback icon tokens communicate status and semantic meaning within contextual components such as alerts, inline messages, notifications, and system states.

Unlike core icon tokens, which express hierarchy, feedback icon tokens convey semantic intent — success, warning, error, or informational states. They are always paired with corresponding feedback surfaces to maintain clarity, accessibility, and visual consistency.
Icon used to communicate positive status or confirmation.
Icon used to signal caution or attention-required states.
Icon used to communicate errors, critical issues, or destructive outcomes.
Icon used to present neutral or informational guidance.
Icon color for neutral feedback states.
Default icon color for inline links.
Icon color when a link is hovered.
Icon color when a link is pressed or active.

Shadow tokens define elevation and depth across the interface. They create visual separation between layers — such as surfaces, overlays, and floating elements — helping users understand hierarchy, grouping, and interactive affordances.

Shadows are role-based and independent of specific components, allowing elevation patterns to scale consistently across themes and layouts.
Low-emphasis shadow color for subtle elevation cues (5% opacity).
Higher-emphasis shadow color for prominent depth separation (20% opacity).
Focus ring shadow color for interactive element focus states (blue 10% opacity).
Error/danger focus ring shadow color (red 10% opacity).
Warning focus ring shadow color for caution-state elements (orange 10% opacity).
Success focus ring shadow color (green 20% opacity).
Info focus ring shadow color (turquoise 20% opacity).
Neutral focus ring shadow color (20% opacity).

These controls typically use minimal or transparent backgrounds and rely on text and icon color to communicate interactivity.

Tertiary actions are the lowest-emphasis interactive controls, using no background or border. They appear as text-only or icon-only buttons for supplementary actions like "Cancel", "Learn more", or inline links. They share the same state pattern as secondary but with fully transparent backgrounds across all states except disabled.

Category colors define a distinct set of hues used to represent different groups or entities in charts and data visualizations. Each category color provides clear visual separation while maintaining balance and accessibility across the palette.

Each category comes in two tones — strong for prominent chart marks like lines, bars, and points, and subtle for backgrounds, ranges, and de-emphasized fills.

These colors should be used consistently to represent the same category across charts, dashboards, and data contexts.
First categorical color, in its strong tone. Used for prominent chart marks like lines, bars, and points.
First categorical color, in its subtle tone. Used for backgrounds, ranges, and de-emphasized fills.
Second categorical color, in its strong tone. Used for prominent chart marks like lines, bars, and points.
Second categorical color, in its subtle tone. Used for backgrounds, ranges, and de-emphasized fills.

Scale colors define sequential color ranges used to represent numeric values. These tokens provide a smooth progression from low to high intensity, enabling clear visual representation of magnitude, density, or progression in charts and heatmaps.

Sequential scales should be applied consistently so that lighter colors represent lower values and darker colors represent higher values.
Lightest value in the sequential data scale.
Low value in the sequential data scale.
Moderate-low value in the sequential data scale.
Mid value in the sequential data scale.
Neutral midpoint of the sequential data scale.
Moderate-high value in the sequential data scale.
High value in the sequential data scale.
Very high value in the sequential data scale.
Highest intensity in the sequential data scale.

Delta colors represent directional change in data visualizations. They communicate increases, decreases, and neutral states using color intensity while preserving meaning across light and dark themes.

Delta tokens are commonly used in charts, indicators, and metrics to visualize performance changes, trends, or comparisons.
Used when a value shows no meaningful increase or decrease. Represents stable or unchanged data.
